labels.og_answer: Brachiosaurus was about 22 to 25 m (72 to 82 ft) long, by a reconstruction

top.answer: Brachiosaurus was about 22 to 25 m (72 to 82 ft) long and roughly 30 to 45 tonnes, both rebuilt from one partial skeleton. The height of Brachiosaurus was never measured, since that skeleton has no neck: rebuilt, its head would stand about 7 m (23 ft) up with the neck level, over 14 m (46 ft) with it straight up. Our model is built at the size of that one skeleton, kept in Chicago, from an animal probably still growing. With the neck raised as we chose it, the head stands about seven people up and the shoulders about four.
top.answer_more: Berlin's famous skeleton, its skull about 13 m (43 ft) up, is its African relative Giraffatitan in a show pose. Most pictures of Brachiosaurus show that relative too.

scale.what: Our Brachiosaurus beside a person 1.70 m tall, to one scale, at the size of the one skeleton the name rests on, dug up in Colorado in 1900. Neck, head, lower legs and most of the tail follow Giraffatitan and other finds. The head stands 11.5 m (38 ft) up only by the neck angle we chose: that height is ours, not a finding.

guess.q: What did Riggs's team first take its upper arm bone for?
guess.a: A crushed thigh bone of a long-necked dinosaur they already knew, and the find was nearly passed over. Only the ribs beside it, far too big for that animal, kept them digging, and the real thigh bone, almost as long, turned up soon after.

blocks.nav: How tall was Brachiosaurus, and was it the tallest dinosaur?
blocks.h: How tall was Brachiosaurus, and was it the tallest dinosaur?
paras: Nobody can say to the metre: the Chicago skeleton has no neck, and the two neck bones found elsewhere may not even be Brachiosaurus. So every head height in print was drawn on Giraffatitan's neck, none measured.

How it held that neck is argued, and the middle view is raised, neither level nor straight up. Our model's neck rises at about 41 degrees, its head top 11.5 m (38 ft) up. The same body would hold its head about 7 m (23 ft) up with a level neck, over 14 m (46 ft) with it straight up. The tallest mounted dinosaur skeleton is that Berlin Giraffatitan, and which dinosaur stood tallest in life is not known for sure: the biggest dinosaurs page takes up that question.

blocks.nav: The Brachiosaurus skeleton: what was found
blocks.h: The Brachiosaurus skeleton: what was found
paras: In 1900 a team from the Field Columbian Museum led by Elmer Riggs dug the skeleton out near Grand Junction in western Colorado. After the body was partly buried, a stream carried off its front part. In 1903 Riggs named it Brachiosaurus altithorax, arm lizard with a high chest, for its long upper arm bone and deep trunk. One shoulder bone had not finished growing, so the animal was probably still growing too. The Field Museum in Chicago keeps the bones, and the big skeletons it put up for visitors are casts, partly sculpted after Giraffatitan.

points: Seven back vertebrae, the sacrum and the first two tail vertebrae.
The right upper arm bone, 2.04 m (6.7 ft) as preserved, its lower end lost, and the right thigh bone, 2.03 m (6.7 ft).
The right hip blade and a piece of the left, the left coracoid (a shoulder bone) and five ribs, none complete.
The head: after a skull found in Colorado in 1883, only tentatively this species, its missing parts, the nose arch among them, restored.
Neck, front of the back, shoulder blades, forearms, hands, shins, feet and the tail behind its first two bones: mostly after Giraffatitan.
The left upper arm and thigh bones: mirrors of the right.

end: So our Brachiosaurus has the size of one animal and the parts of several.

scale.what: Our Brachiosaurus as a skeleton from the right, coloured by where each bone comes from.
scale.alt: Our Brachiosaurus as a skeleton from the right, a few cream bones in the back, hips, one thigh and one upper arm among blue, orange and brown ones, beside the grey person.

key.text: Cream: its own bones, found in Colorado in 1900: seven back vertebrae, the sacrum, two tail vertebrae, the right hip blade, thigh bone and upper arm bone, and three ribs in view.

Blue: its own bones mirrored or completed: the left upper arm and thigh bones as mirrors of the right, the upper arm bone's lost end, the ribs' lower parts. The shoulder bone in view is a mirror too: the one found is the left, behind it.
Orange: after other American finds, above all a skull found in Colorado in 1883, only tentatively this species, its missing parts, the nose arch among them, restored, and one forearm bone.
Brown: after Giraffatitan, all the rest: neck, front of the back, shoulder blades, most of the lower legs, ribs and tail.

blocks.nav: Giraffatitan, the famous one in Berlin
blocks.h: Giraffatitan, the famous one in Berlin
paras: Giraffatitan brancai is the tall skeleton in Berlin's Museum für Naturkunde. Its bones were dug at Tendaguru in what is now Tanzania from 1909 to 1913, under German colonial rule, as the museum itself says. Named Brachiosaurus brancai in 1914, it got its own genus in 2009, when a study counted at least 26 differences from the American animal. The mount combines several animals, its neck and skull are plaster, and most of its real bone is in the legs, hips and ribs. It is about 23 m (75 ft) long, its skull about 13 m (43 ft) up since the remount of 2007, 12 m as built in 1937, the neck now nearly upright for show. Most pictures of Brachiosaurus follow this better-known relative.

The front legs were longer than the hind legs, so the back sloped up to the shoulders, as in its relatives, and the long arms gave it its name. The trunk was deep and about a quarter longer than Giraffatitan's, by its own back bones. The tail was tall at its base, probably long, and carried off the ground like other sauropods'.

The neck is borrowed from Giraffatitan, raised in ours in a gentle curve, though the angle is argued. The head follows the Colorado skull of 1883, its missing nose arch restored low, the fleshy nostrils low and far forward on the snout.
No brachiosaurid skin has been found. Ours shows small flat scales like other sauropods, and its colour is a choice, because none is known.

blocks.nav: Brachiosaurus vs a giraffe, and vs Argentinosaurus
blocks.h: Brachiosaurus vs a giraffe, and vs Argentinosaurus
paras: A giraffe bull stands up to about 5.5 m (18 ft) and weighs up to about 1.4 tonnes. Our model's head is about twice as high, its shoulders alone rise above a tall giraffe's head, and roughly 30 to 45 tonnes is about 22 to 33 giraffe bulls. Argentinosaurus was bigger: about 30 to 35 m (98 to 115 ft) long and roughly 65 to 80 tonnes, both rebuilt, against about 22 to 25 m and 30 to 45 tonnes. The two never met, tens of millions of years and a continent apart, and our two models hold their heads at almost the same height only because of the necks we chose.

Brachiosaurus lived in the Late Jurassic of western North America, about 150 million years ago, where the rocks of the Morrison Formation now lie. It lived on land: Riggs argued that in 1904 from its legs and feet, against the old picture of a swamp animal. The range a museum gives for the genus stops at about 145 million years ago.
Two things decide every number on this page.

points: The length and the weight are rebuilt:
no whole skeleton exists, so both rest on Giraffatitan's frame and a chosen density.
Ours is one model, not the species:
its 24.0 m along the backbone and its head at 11.5 m are the model's own numbers, the head's from the neck we chose, never the animal's.

rows.text: A range many sites give. Such lengths mostly copy the proportions of Giraffatitan, its African relative, and several of them are older than a study of 2009. That study found the American animal's trunk about 23 percent longer than Giraffatitan's and its tail 20 to 25 percent longer. With those proportions, the length comes to about 22 to 25 m.
A figure of 1962 from a small model dipped in water, and the model showed the Berlin species, not this one. Later work set it aside as an outlier.
The Berlin exhibition's label of 2007, for Giraffatitan. Those who remounted it put the true figure well below, and newer models of the mount give about 23 to 38 tonnes.

Both are the Berlin mount, a Giraffatitan. Its skull stood 11.87 m up as built in 1937, with the neck leaning forward, and about 13 m since the remount of 2007, with the neck nearly upright, a pose chosen for its effect on visitors. The American animal's height was never measured.
Riggs's own title for it, in 1901 and 1903, and true then. The far heavier titanosaurs, Argentinosaurus among them, were found later.

rows.term: A swamp animal, held up by the water
rows.text: The old picture of all long-necked dinosaurs. Riggs argued against it in 1904 from the legs and feet. Today it is set aside.

rows.term: Nostrils on top of the head
rows.text: Old restorations put the fleshy nostril at the top of the big bony opening in the skull. A study of 2001 found it sat far forward on the snout.

blocks.intro: For each picture: where it came from, and what we know now.

rows.term: A tail lying on the ground
rows.text: Berlin's famous skeleton, a Giraffatitan, was mounted that way in 1937, and its tail has hung in the air since the remount of 2007. Sauropods carried their tails off the ground, and museums show them so today.

rows.term: Rearing up on its hind legs to reach the treetops
rows.text: Probably not. Its front legs were longer than its hind legs, and a model of its African relative puts the body's weight far forward.

rows.term: Round front feet, like an elephant's
rows.text: Going by its relatives' hands and by tracks, each front foot was most likely a tall half tube of five long bones with one small thumb claw, leaving a horseshoe-shaped print.

rows.term: Brown, grey or speckled skin, shown as if known
rows.text: A 2025 study claimed to find colour in the skin of a young Diplodocus, another sauropod, and a reply in 2026 found the claim not backed by the data. So the colour of Brachiosaurus is still unknown.

items.a: Leaves of tall trees, conifers and tree ferns among them, says the Natural History Museum in London. It did not chew: the leaves were broken down in its gut, as in other sauropods.

No. Argentinosaurus was longer and much heavier: about 30 to 35 m (98 to 115 ft) and roughly 65 to 80 tonnes, both rebuilt. Which dinosaur was the biggest of all is still open, and the biggest dinosaurs page takes up that question.

items.line: A large adult T. rex was about 12 m long, about 4 m at the hips and roughly 8 to 9 tonnes. Our T. rex is built to SUE's measurements and stands beside a person to one scale, with a list of what was found of SUE.

items.alt: Our woolly mammoth, the Berezovka bull, from the side in a dark brown coat: high domed head, sloping back, two curved tusks, and a mark at his shoulder, 271 cm (8.9 ft) by a reconstruction. The grey person beside him, 1.70 m tall, stands lower than the tusk tips.
items.line: A typical Siberian bull stood about 2.7 to 2.9 m at the shoulder and weighed about 4 to 5 tonnes. Our woolly mammoth is one real bull found frozen in 1900, 2.71 m at the shoulder by a reconstruction, beside a person to one scale.
